question: A CXR in a 4-year-old with fever shows right lower lobe consolidation with blunting of the costophrenic angle. Ultrasound confirms a free-flowing pleural effusion. What is the most appropriate next step?

answers.text: Continue IV antibiotics and repeat CXR at 4 weeks without further imaging

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A free-flowing effusion in a febrile child requires assessment of size and response. Ultrasound-guided aspiration or intercostal drain may be needed if the effusion is large or there is no improvement.

answers.text: Perform ultrasound-guided pleural aspiration for diagnostic and/or therapeutic drainage based on effusion size and clinical course

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Ultrasound-guided drainage is indicated when effusion is significant or the child does not improve on antibiotics. Ultrasound characterises the fluid (free vs loculated) and guides safe aspiration.

answers.text: Proceed immediately to VATS (video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery) without aspiration

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: VATS is reserved for organised empyema not responding to drainage. Free-flowing effusion is first managed with ultrasound-guided aspiration and IV antibiotics.

answers.text: Order a CT chest with contrast to stage the complication before any drainage

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CT adds significant radiation and is not needed before drainage of a clearly visible ultrasound-confirmed effusion. CT is reserved for parenchymal complications not resolved by initial management.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the imaging-to-management pathway: confirmed effusion → ultrasound characterisation → guided drainage if indicated, before considering CT or surgery.
Exactly right. Ultrasound guides both the diagnosis and the drainage — it is the pivotal tool in paediatric pleural effusion management.
